title: Geometry-Controlled Exceptional Points in Helicoidal Orbital-Angular-Momentum Photonics
abstract: Exceptional points (EPs) are non-Hermitian spectral singularities where eigenvalues and eigenvectors coalesce. We propose a geometry-controlled route to EPs in orbital-angular-momentum (OAM) photonics. In an effective torsion-free helicoidal background, the twist supplies a signed, real chiral splitting between opposite-OAM modes, while openness, gain, loss, leakage, or channel coupling, supplies the non-Hermiticity. The EP is reached when the geometric detuning compensates for a residual mode splitting and the linewidth contrast meets the non-Hermitian balance condition; the twist rate is thus the control parameter, not the source of non-Hermiticity. We obtain the OAM slope both for a confined quantum problem and, in the paraxial regime, for a helically twisted guide, and embed the OAM doublet in a multimode mode-space model to show that the EP survives spectator modes. Eigenvalue coalescence, phase-rigidity collapse, linear EP tracking with residual detuning, and branch exchange under geometric encircling provide falsifiable signatures. An OAM-resolved input-output response maps these onto spectroscopy-level observables, including spectral maps and three-dimensional Riemann-surface visualizations. A device-level paraxial simulation of two distinct photonic platforms, one reciprocal and one asymmetric-coupling Wiersig-type platform, reproduces the predicted exceptional point and its linear geometric tracking.
summary: The paper presents a comprehensive theoretical and simulation study on controlling Exceptional Points (EPs) in OAM photonics using the geometry of a helicoidal waveguide. By tuning the twist rate ($\Omega$), researchers can force the system into an EP, which is confirmed by observing characteristic signatures like eigenvalue coalescence and phase rigidity collapse. This provides a robust blueprint for designing next-generation photonic devices based on non-Hermitian physics.
main_problem: The paper proposes a novel method to control Exceptional Points (EPs) in Orbital-Angular-Momentum (OAM) photonics using geometric parameters derived from the helicoidal background.
main_result: They demonstrate that the EP location can be precisely tuned by controlling the geometry (twist rate $\Omega$), providing measurable, falsifiable signatures like linear tracking of the EP with residual detuning.
method: The analysis involves reducing the wave dynamics to an effective two-mode non-Hermitian Hamiltonian and applying input-output formalism to map theoretical predictions onto observable spectral maps.
model_or_system: The system is modeled using OAM modes propagating in a helicoidal background, governed by an effective Schrödinger equation derived from the Laplace-Beltrami operator. The dynamics are captured by an effective two-mode Hamiltonian describing coupling between opposite-OAM modes ($\pm m$).
key_observables: Eigenvalue coalescence, phase-rigidity collapse ($r_j 	o 0$), linear tracking of $	ext{EP}$ vs. residual detuning ($\Delta_0$), and branch exchange upon parameter looping.
important_parameters: The helicoidal twist rate ($\Omega$ or $	au$) acts as the primary control parameter, compensating for a residual detuning ($\Delta_0$). The EP condition requires balancing geometric detuning with non-Hermitian losses/gains ($|\Delta\gamma| \sim 4|g|$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on reducing the system to an isolated two-mode doublet, assuming spectator modes remain spectrally separated. It primarily uses semiclassical or coupled-mode approximations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the coalescence of eigenvalue branches (Fig. 2), the collapse of phase rigidity at the EP (Fig. 5), and the linear relationship between $	ext{EP}$ location and external detuning ($\Delta_0$) (Fig. 6, Fig. 10c).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from deriving the effective Hamiltonian in a helicoidal background to establishing the EP condition via two-mode reduction. It then validates this using multimode spectral tests, introduces advanced diagnostics like phase rigidity and topological looping, and concludes with device simulations on both reciprocal and asymmetric coupling platforms.
why_interesting: This work bridges geometric control (topology/geometry) with non-Hermitian physics in photonics, offering a highly controllable platform for realizing exotic quantum phenomena that are relevant to integrated quantum optics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Conceptual structure of a geometry-controlled exceptional point. (a) A helicoidal channel or effective helicoidal medium couples axial and azimuthal motion through the twist parameter Ω. (b) Projection onto two opposite-OAM modes gives a non- Hermitian two-mode problem with coupling g, linewidths γ+m and γ−m, and real detuning ∆(Ω) = ∆0 −αmΩ.

FIG. 2. Dimensionless eigenvalue branches near a geometry-controlled exceptional point. The plotted quantity is ˜λ± = (λ± −E0 + i¯γ/2)/g for g = 0.10 meV, ∆γ = 4g, and ∆(Ω) = ∆0(1 −Ω/ΩEP). The two eigenvalues and eigenvectors coalesce at Ω= ΩEP.

FIG. 3. Exceptional-point condition in the reciprocal model. The discriminant D = (∆−i∆γ/2)2 + 4g2 vanishes only when the real geometric detuning is compensated, ∆= 0, and the linewidth contrast satisfies |∆γ| = 4|g|. The solid line is Re D = 0, the dashed line is Im D = 0, and the marked intersection gives the exceptional point.

FIG. 4. Multimode OAM-space test of the geometry-controlled EP. (a) Real parts of the eigenvalues of a finite OAM manifold with modes ℓ= −4, . . . , 4. The thick branches are the target ℓ= ±1 doublet, while the thin branches are spectator OAM modes. The target branches coalesce at the calibrated twist even when weak residual couplings to spectator modes are present. (b) Imaginary parts of the two target branches, showing the associated linewidth coalescence.

FIG. 5. Eigenvector-sensitive verification of the geometry-controlled EP. (a) Minimum phase rigidity of the reciprocal complex- symmetric two-mode model as a function of normalized twist. The collapse near Ω= ΩEP indicates eigenvector coalescence rather than a conventional crossing. (b) Corresponding eigenvalue gap, displaying the square root closing at the same twist.
